hints: The node you see on a depth is not always a right child. Which node on each depth is the visible one?
Use level-order BFS: the last node popped on each level is the rightmost one. (Alternatively, a DFS that visits right before left records the first node it meets at each new depth.)

1. If root is null return an empty list.
  2. BFS with a queue; read size at the start of each level.
  3. Pop size nodes, pushing left then right children.
  4. When i == size - 1, add that node's value to the answer.

approaches.name: Brute force
approaches.idea: Collect every level as a full list (level-order traversal), then take the last element of each list.

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.idea: BFS by levels, keeping only the last node of each level instead of storing whole rows.

explain: For [1,2,3,4,null,null,null,8]: level 0 is 1, level 1 is 2 and 3 so we see 3. Level 2 contains only 4 (the left child of 2), and level 3 contains only 8, so both are visible: [1,3,4,8]. This is the edge case to watch: a left-side node is visible when nothing lies to its right on that depth, which is why always following right children fails. An empty tree returns [].
recognize: 'Only the rightmost node on each depth' → level-order BFS keeping the last node of each level.
